- Substitute compensation, actual entitlement and remedy-specific consent: Canonical Decision Record `department_of_the_army_v_blue_fox_merits_1999-01-20.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / The requested lien supplies substitute compensation without an applicable waiver, 1999-01-20; unanimous opinion.

**Present operation effective:** 1999-01-20.

**Exceptions and limits:** Not every equitable lien is money damages. The Miller Act’s bond duty does not make the Government a guarantor when it fails to obtain a bond. Independent reviewability and adequate-remedy conditions are not eliminated.

**Holdings navigation:** [Department of the Army v. Blue Fox, Inc. — The requested lien supplies substitute compensation without an applicable waiver](HOLDINGS.md#the-requested-lien-supplies-substitute-compensation-without-an-applicable-waiver-1).

### Ripeness of an announced administrative enforcement forum

**Governing question:** Whether a definite agency announcement of possible enforcement authority is immediately fit for judicial resolution.

**Current rule:** Completeness of an agency position and predominantly legal character of a dispute do not alone establish ripeness. A general announcement of a possible enforcement forum that directs no present change in primary conduct, determines no particular liability and permits meaningful review of concrete application is not ripe merely because a future complaint may require defense or forum allocation is uncertain. Finality, standing, fitness and hardship remain distinct inquiries.

**Authority by component:**

- Present conduct consequences, review opportunity and independent ripeness inquiry: Canonical Decision Record `att_corp_v_iowa_utilities_board_merits_1999-01-25.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / XII. The general section 208 announcement is not ripe for review, 1999-01-25; eight Associates directly join.

**Present operation effective:** 1999-01-25.

**Exceptions and limits:** A presently binding or burdensome statement presents a different question. This rule creates no universal exhaustion requirement or promise of future standing and timeliness, and does not defer every challenge until penalties are collected.

**Holdings navigation:** [AT&T Corp. v. Iowa Utilities Board — XII. The general section 208 announcement is not ripe for review](HOLDINGS.md#xii-the-general-section-208-announcement-is-not-ripe-for-review-1).

### Common-issue aggregation and meaningful individual defenses

**Governing question:** Due-process conditions for state consolidation of genuinely common issues.

**Current rule:** A State may try genuinely common issues together only if each defendant can meaningfully contest the evidence and every material defense to those issues, with remaining claimant-specific elements still required. Party numbers and omission of brand names from a verdict form do not alone establish a violation, but efficiency cannot replace legally necessary individual proof. Representative trial plaintiffs do not statistically establish other claimants’ exposure, causation, injury or damages, and a product category cannot decide a materially different characteristic without fair adjudication. Later proceedings may apply only the common findings lawfully resolved; a later individual trial cannot cure a material defense already foreclosed.

**Authority by component:**

- Actual common issue, meaningful defense, individual proof and scope of later findings: Canonical Decision Record `john_crane_inc_v_abate_merits_1999-02-18.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / I. Common issues may be tried together only with a meaningful defense; III. The affirmance preserves individual proof and distinct remedies, 1999-02-18; unanimous opinion.

**Present operation effective:** 1999-02-18.

**Exceptions and limits:** No numerical ceiling, brand-name-verdict rule, authority to bind strangers or categorical appellate cure follows. The actual procedural device’s requirements govern; federal settlement-class rules are not automatically imported into state consolidation.

**Holdings navigation:** [John Crane, Inc. v. Abate — I. Common issues may be tried together only with a meaningful defense](HOLDINGS.md#i-common-issues-may-be-tried-together-only-with-a-meaningful-defense-1); [John Crane, Inc. v. Abate — III. The affirmance preserves individual proof and distinct remedies](HOLDINGS.md#iii-the-affirmance-preserves-individual-proof-and-distinct-remedies).

### Special statutory tribunals for election-financing challenges

**Governing question:** When a constitutional election-financing claim must enter FECA’s or the Fund Act’s special statutory tribunal.

**Current rule:** A claim lacking Article III standing or presenting a constitutional theory plainly foreclosed by controlling law may be rejected before invoking the extraordinary statutory tribunal. A live substantial constitutional question cannot be bypassed because the court expects it to fail. A substantial qualifying FECA constitutional question brought by an authorized plaintiff follows §437h to the court of appeals sitting en banc. A substantial Fund Act implementation or construction claim follows §9011(b) to a three-judge district court with direct Supreme Court appeal and no administrative-exhaustion requirement. Section 9011(a)’s thirty-day D.C. Circuit review of Commission action remains a separate route. Statutory eligibility to bring suit does not establish Article III standing on each claim.

**Authority by component:**

- National Committee of the Reform Party v. Democratic National Committee — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “IV. The granted claims supply no basis for bypassing or requiring a different statutory tribunal”, 1999-03-17; Thomas, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer.

**Present operation effective:** Reform Party, March 17, 1999.

**Holdings navigation:** [National Committee of the Reform Party of the United States of America v. Democratic National Committee — IV. The granted claims supply no basis for bypassing or requiring a different statutory tribunal](HOLDINGS.md#iv-the-granted-claims-supply-no-basis-for-bypassing-or-requiring-a-different-statutory-tribunal).

### Supreme Court review of state judgments despite sovereign immunity

**Governing question:** Whether State immunity prevents Supreme Court review of a state court’s resolution of federal questions.

**Current rule:** The Eleventh Amendment does not prevent Supreme Court review under 28 U.S.C. §1257 of federal questions decided in a State’s own courts. That appellate review is distinct from initiating a new federal damages action against the State.

**Authority by component:**

- South Central Bell Telephone Co. v. Alabama — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “I. The Eleventh Amendment does not bar review of Alabama’s own judgment”, 1999-03-23; Stone-Zsela Part I, all nine Justices.

**Present operation effective:** South Central Bell, March 23, 1999.

**Holdings navigation:** [South Central Bell Telephone Co. v. Alabama — The Eleventh Amendment does not bar review of Alabama's own judgment](HOLDINGS.md#the-eleventh-amendment-does-not-bar-review-of-alabamas-own-judgment-1).

### Formal process and the original removal period

**Governing question:** When §1446(b)’s original-pleading thirty-day removal period begins.

**Current rule:** An informal courtesy copy received before formal service, waiver or legally equivalent process subjects the defendant to court authority does not itself start the original-pleading removal period. Under the first branch, thirty days run once both that process requirement and receipt, through service or otherwise, of the initial pleading setting forth the claim for relief occur. The separate branch runs thirty days after summons service if the initial pleading is then filed in court and need not be served on the defendant; the shorter applicable period controls. If the complaint arrives first, later process starts the first branch; if process precedes required pleading receipt, that branch awaits receipt.

**Authority by component:**

- Murphy Brothers, Inc. v. Michetti Pipe Stringing, Inc. — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “Formal process and the statutory pleading events govern the original removal period”, 1999-04-05; Ginsburg’s seven-Justice Opinion of the Court.

**Present operation effective:** Murphy Brothers, April 5, 1999.

**Exceptions and limits:** No validly begun period is extended and service evasion is not excused. Removal before service is not prohibited. The later-removability paragraph, unpresented waiver timing and other process sequences are not decided; timeliness does not establish subject-matter jurisdiction.

**Holdings navigation:** [Murphy Brothers, Inc. v. Michetti Pipe Stringing, Inc. — Formal process and the statutory pleading events govern the original removal period](HOLDINGS.md#formal-process-and-the-statutory-pleading-events-govern-the-original-removal-period-1).

### Classwide relief under Rule 23(b)(2)

**Governing question:** When a proposed injunctive or corresponding declaratory class satisfies Rule 23(b)(2).

**Current rule:** Together with Rule 23(a), Rule 23(b)(2) requires a supported showing that generally applicable defendant conduct makes final injunctive or corresponding declaratory relief appropriate for the proposed class. A common product, course of conduct or request for monitoring does not alone establish that showing. Courts must connect material differences among members to actual entitlement to the requested classwide relief and preservation of individual proof and substantive defenses. Rule 23(b)(3)’s predominance and superiority requirements are not imported into (b)(2); individual differences alone do not categorically defeat certification.

**Authority by component:**

- Barnes v. American Tobacco Co. — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “The proposed monitoring class does not satisfy the applicable classwide-relief requirement”, 1999-04-07; Breyer, all nine Justices.

**Present operation effective:** Barnes, April 7, 1999.

**Exceptions and limits:** No categorical medical-monitoring prohibition or additional universal indivisibility condition is adopted. Applicable Rule 23(a) requirements and substantive defenses remain; an equitable label does not establish classwide entitlement.

**Holdings navigation:** [Barnes v. American Tobacco Co. — The proposed monitoring class does not satisfy the applicable classwide-relief requirement](HOLDINGS.md#the-proposed-monitoring-class-does-not-satisfy-the-applicable-classwide-relief-requirement-1).

### Price-Anderson coverage before tribal exhaustion

**Governing question:** Who decides Price-Anderson public-liability coverage before prudential tribal exhaustion.

**Current rule:** When an invoked Price-Anderson federal proceeding requires deciding whether pleaded claims are covered public-liability actions, the federal court must decide coverage before imposing prudential tribal exhaustion. Covered claims follow the Act’s specific federal channel; uncovered claims retain their own jurisdictional, tribal-authority and exhaustion analysis. Ordinary comity cannot postpone this specifically assigned federal coverage task.

**Authority by component:**

- El Paso Natural Gas Co. v. Neztsosie — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “Federal courts determine Price-Anderson coverage before imposing tribal exhaustion”, 1999-05-03; Thomas, all nine Justices.

**Present operation effective:** El Paso Natural Gas, May 3, 1999.

**Exceptions and limits:** The state-court removal text is not rewritten to authorize tribal-court removal. Coverage is not established merely by allegations of mining injury, and exhaustion itself supplies no tribal substantive authority.

**Holdings navigation:** [El Paso Natural Gas Co. v. Neztsosie — Federal courts determine Price-Anderson coverage before imposing tribal exhaustion](HOLDINGS.md#federal-courts-determine-price-anderson-coverage-before-imposing-tribal-exhaustion-1).

### Cross-appeals and enlargement of the decree

**Governing question:** When an appellee needs a cross-appeal rather than an alternative ground for affirmance.

**Current rule:** An appellee may defend the existing decree on an alternative preserved ground but may not, without a cross-appeal, enlarge its own rights or reduce the appellant’s rights under that decree. Invoking comity does not turn a defense of the judgment into an appeal for a more favorable one.

**Authority by component:**

- El Paso Natural Gas Co. v. Neztsosie — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “Nonappealing appellees may defend a decree but may not enlarge it”, 1999-05-03; Thomas, all nine Justices.

**Present operation effective:** El Paso Natural Gas, May 3, 1999.

**Open question:** The Court does not classify every omission as jurisdictional or decide every possible exception, including an independent jurisdictional defect requiring a different disposition.

**Holdings navigation:** [El Paso Natural Gas Co. v. Neztsosie — Nonappealing appellees may defend a decree but may not enlarge it](HOLDINGS.md#nonappealing-appellees-may-defend-a-decree-but-may-not-enlarge-it-1).

### Military appellate writs and independently conferred jurisdiction

**Governing question:** Whether the All Writs Act permits military appellate supervision of separate executive personnel actions.

**Current rule:** The All Writs Act permits protection of independently conferred military appellate jurisdiction over court-martial findings and sentences. It supplies no jurisdiction to enjoin a separate executive personnel action outside that review merely because the action follows a court-martial conviction. Writs genuinely needed to protect or enforce a lawful military appellate judgment remain available.

**Authority by component:**

- Clinton v. Goldsmith — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “A writ cannot enlarge military appellate jurisdiction”, 1999-05-17; Kennedy, all nine Justices.

**Present operation effective:** Goldsmith, May 17, 1999.

**Open question:** The constitutional merits of the personnel action and the adequacy or availability of a particular outside remedy are not decided.

**Holdings navigation:** [Clinton v. Goldsmith — A writ cannot enlarge military appellate jurisdiction](HOLDINGS.md#a-writ-cannot-enlarge-military-appellate-jurisdiction-1).

### One complete ordinary state-review round under former §2254

**Governing question:** What state review a prisoner must complete under the pre-AEDPA exhaustion law.

**Current rule:** Each federal claim must be fairly presented through one complete round of the State’s established ordinary appellate process, including discretionary review in its highest court when that petition is an ordinary available step. Selective acceptance or unlikely success does not make the filing unavailable. Actual state-law unavailability and the former statute’s absent-process and ineffective-process exceptions remain. Omission of a required step whose opportunity has expired produces procedural default, subject to the existing cause-and-prejudice and actual-innocence gateways, rather than an unexhausted still-available remedy.

**Authority by component:**

- O’Sullivan v. Boerckel — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “I. An available ordinary discretionary petition is part of one complete round”, 1999-06-07; Souter Parts I–II with Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas. Part II supplies expiration/default classification; Part III’s five-Justice reservation excludes Stone-Zsela.

**Present operation effective:** O’Sullivan, June 7, 1999.

**Exceptions and limits:** Every extraordinary remedy, repetitive collateral presentation after a complete round and a petition to the Supreme Court are not required by this rule. Former chapter 153 governs the source application; amended statutory provisions retain their own temporal scope.

**Open question:** The effect of an express State opt-out retaining occasional discretionary review remains unresolved; no universal formula for such an opt-out is adopted.

**Holdings navigation:** [O'Sullivan v. Boerckel — I. An available ordinary discretionary petition is part of one complete round](HOLDINGS.md#i-an-available-ordinary-discretionary-petition-is-part-of-one-complete-round-1).

### Interlocutory review of monetary discovery sanctions against counsel

**Governing question:** Whether counsel may immediately appeal a monetary Rule 37 sanction during ongoing litigation.

**Current rule:** A monetary Rule 37 discovery sanction against counsel during ongoing litigation is not immediately appealable under §1291’s collateral-order doctrine merely because representation has ended. At the category level, review of discovery relevance, responses and compliance remains intertwined with the merits and litigation record. Independently, the personally sanctioned attorney can seek effective review after final judgment despite no longer representing the client; ordinary payment, delay and reputational burdens do not establish an irretrievably lost right requiring immediate review.

**Authority by component:**

- Cunningham v. Hamilton County — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “Complete separation from the merits”, 1999-06-14; all nine Justices. That holding supplies the independent separation failure; “Effective review after final judgment” supplies the independent reviewability ground.

**Present operation effective:** Cunningham, June 14, 1999.

**Exceptions and limits:** Materially different independent nonparty finality, other sanctions regimes and independently final contempt remain unresolved. Section 1292(b), mandamus and proper contempt routes retain their own requirements.

**Holdings navigation:** [Cunningham v. Hamilton County — Complete separation from the merits](HOLDINGS.md#complete-separation-from-the-merits-1); [Cunningham v. Hamilton County — Effective review after final judgment](HOLDINGS.md#effective-review-after-final-judgment).

### Unsecured-creditor prejudgment asset restraints

**Governing question:** Whether general federal equity permits freezing unencumbered assets to secure a purely monetary unsecured claim.

**Current rule:** A federal court may not use general equitable authority to freeze unencumbered assets before judgment for a general unsecured creditor suing solely for money damages without a lien, equitable interest, statutory authorization or other recognized source of prejudgment control. Likely success and threatened collection difficulty do not supply that power. Rule 65 regulates procedure; Rule 64 preserves independently authorized security routes without creating the missing substantive authority.

**Authority by component:**

- Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo, S.A. v. Alliance Bond Fund, Inc. — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “General equity does not supply this unsecured-creditor asset freeze”, 1999-06-17; Scalia with Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Kennedy and Thomas.

**Present operation effective:** Grupo Mexicano, June 17, 1999.

**Exceptions and limits:** Specific property in dispute, statutory freezes, independently authorized fraudulent-transfer relief, bankruptcy orders, Rule 64 attachment and postjudgment enforcement retain their own bases. No bond liability, damages or lien is established.

**Sequence or decisionmaker:** A distinct challenge to legal authority during the preliminary period may remain live after final contract success and permanent conversion when asserted preliminary injury and an existing bond preserve consequential relief; a bond alone is not conclusive. Grupo Mexicano Part I, all nine Justices, supplies this bounded continuation.

**Holdings navigation:** [Grupo Mexicano de Desarrollo, S.A. v. Alliance Bond Fund, Inc. — General equity does not supply this unsecured-creditor asset freeze](HOLDINGS.md#general-equity-does-not-supply-this-unsecured-creditor-asset-freeze).

### Federal-judge removal of work-linked collection actions

**Governing question:** When a federal judge may remove a collection action under the event-applicable §1442(a)(3).

**Current rule:** A federal judge may remove a collection action having the required connection to official duties when asserting a colorable federal defense. A levy legally linked to performance of federal judicial work and an official-duty immunity defense can satisfy those conditions even if the defense later fails. Federal employment or a compensation measure alone does not authorize removal of every personal obligation.

**Authority by component:**

- Jefferson County v. Acker — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “Federal-officer removal is proper for these collection actions”, 1999-06-21; Ginsburg Part I with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy and Breyer.

**Present operation effective:** Acker, June 21, 1999.

**Exceptions and limits:** The rule uses the event-applicable text and imports no later expansion. A colorable defense determines the forum without establishing substantive immunity.

**Holdings navigation:** [Jefferson County v. Acker — Federal-officer removal is proper for these collection actions](HOLDINGS.md#federal-officer-removal-is-proper-for-these-collection-actions-1).

### Mandatory limited-fund settlement classes

**Governing question:** What supports contested Rule 23(b)(1)(B) certification on a limited-fund rationale.

**Current rule:** The asserted limit must exist independently of the parties’ negotiated ceiling. Proponents must demonstrate an ascertained maximum insufficient for aggregate claims. The traditional characteristics—a definitely ascertained inadequate fund, devotion of the whole qualifying fund to those claims and equitable treatment of claimants sharing the relevant theory of recovery—are presumptively necessary; proponents must justify a departure. Settlement desirability and predicted eventual depletion do not establish their own maximum or replace applicable Rule 23(a) and (b)(1)(B) requirements.

**Authority by component:**

- Ortiz v. Fibreboard Corp. — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, “2. An independent maximum and the qualified traditional limited-fund framework”, 1999-06-23; Thomas Part II-A with Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg. Seven votes supply independent limit and aggregate insufficiency; Part II-B with O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg supplies the six-vote presumptive characteristics and justified-departure burden. Stone-Zsela’s stronger whole-fund condition is not counted.

**Present operation effective:** Ortiz, June 23, 1999.

**Exceptions and limits:** Rule 23(b)(3) predominance is not imported. No previously segregated asset, certain insolvency, mechanical equality overriding valid priorities or exclusive bankruptcy route is invariably required. Materially conflicting present/future or insurance allocation interests retain the independent-representation requirement; fairness review does not replace protection in negotiation.

**Open question:** The full range of justified departures and whether unliquidated mass-tort claims can ever satisfy the category remain unresolved. No universal exhaustion probability, opt-out right, whole-company retention prohibition or replacement agreement is adopted.

**Related current rules:** Certification of settlement-only classes retains Amchem’s applicable-prerequisite and independent-representation rules. Ortiz applies their bounded logically antecedent nonmerits sequence without assuming jurisdiction to decide individual substantive claims.

**Holdings navigation:** [Ortiz v. Fibreboard Corp. — 2. An independent maximum and the qualified traditional limited-fund framework](HOLDINGS.md#2-an-independent-maximum-and-the-qualified-traditional-limited-fund-framework).

### Deterrent civil penalties as Article III redress

**Governing question:** When a statutory civil penalty payable to the Treasury redresses the plaintiff's personal injury.

**Current rule:** A Treasury-payable civil penalty can supply redress when it is likely to deter continuing or reasonably recurring violations that threaten the plaintiff's supported personal interests. The plaintiff need not receive the money. Punishment for wholly past conduct without a remaining personal remedial connection, satisfaction from punishment, and fees alone do not meet this requirement. Deterrence must be supported; it is neither required to be certain nor presumed for every public penalty.

**Authority by component:**

- Preventive redress and its past-conduct boundary: Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw, Public Projection / Holdings / Deterrent penalties can redress supported threatened personal injury, January 12, 2000; O'Connor with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer (seven).

**Present operation effective:** Laidlaw, January 12, 2000.

**Open question:** Survival of a properly initiated penalty claim after proven permanent cessation remains unresolved; Stevens's broader theory is not controlling. Article II objections and statutory diligent-prosecution defenses retain separate predicates.

### Voluntary cessation and continuing controversy

**Governing question:** Whether the defendant's postfiling compliance or cessation ends an initially live controversy.

**Current rule:** A defendant invoking voluntary cessation must make it absolutely clear that the challenged injurious conduct cannot reasonably be expected to recur. Compliance sufficient to defeat an injunction does not by itself meet that burden or negate standing established at commencement. Claimed permanent closure requires evaluation of the actual facts and legal restraints; neither retained legal permission nor dismantling alone determines recurrence.

**Authority by component:**

- Demanding cessation burden and distinction from initial standing or equitable relief: Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw, Public Projection / Holdings / Later compliance does not automatically establish mootness; the closure evidence must be assessed, January 12, 2000; O'Connor with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer (seven).

**Present operation effective:** Laidlaw, January 12, 2000, states the applicable instruction without replacing initial-standing requirements.

**Exceptions and limits:** Fees alone do not preserve a controversy. The rule does not determine that permanent cessation occurred or resolve the reserved survival of a penalty claim after it is proved.

### Appellate judgment after exclusion of trial evidence

**Governing question:** The appellate remedy when correction of an evidentiary admission leaves a verdict unsupported on a preserved Rule 50 motion.

**Current rule:** An appellate court may direct judgment if the legally admissible trial evidence cannot support the verdict on a properly preserved Rule 50 motion, even when insufficiency results from correcting erroneous admission. Rule 50, 28 U.S.C. 2106 and the Seventh Amendment require no automatic retrial because the verdict winner relied on the admission. Before directing judgment, the court must give due consideration to supported new-trial grounds, a fair opportunity to present them and the trial judge's superior position on issues calling for that judgment. It may order retrial, remand the new-trial determination or direct judgment as the circumstances warrant.

**Authority by component:**

- Appellate power and mandatory consideration of supported remedial alternatives: Weisgram v. Marley, Public Projection / Holdings / Appellate judgment may follow correction of erroneous admission; Supported new-trial grounds and fair opportunity remain material, February 22, 2000; Ginsburg for all nine Justices.

**Present operation effective:** Weisgram v. Marley, February 22, 2000.

**Exceptions and limits:** An unexpected change of law, blocked proffer, specific preserved new-trial ground or other procedural unfairness may warrant a different disposition. Reliance on favorable admission and a general possibility of better evidence alone guarantee no second trial. Ordinary preservation limits apply, and original-Rule-702 reliability standards remain unchanged.

**Related current rules:** Claim-specific grounds in renewed Rule 50 motions supplies preservation requirements. Whole-record review of a jury verdict under Rule 50 governs the separate sufficiency assessment.

### Medicare review channels and practical foreclosure of judicial review

**Governing question:** When the Medicare review channel displaces otherwise proper federal-question jurisdiction over arising-under regulatory or payment claims.

**Current rule:** The incorporated section 405(h) channel ordinarily governs Medicare claims, including general procedural or constitutional attacks on regulations; a regulatory label alone does not create an exception. It does not displace otherwise proper 28 U.S.C. 1331 jurisdiction when the actual route offers no safe, practical means of meaningful judicial review and acquiring a reviewable vehicle requires catastrophic exposure. Ordinary expense, delay, exhaustion or hardship while a meaningful route remains realistically available is insufficient. Each claim retains independent ripeness and relief requirements, and the APA supplies no separate jurisdictional grant.

**Authority by component:**

- General channeling and confined practical-foreclosure exception: Shalala v. Illinois Council on Long Term Care, Public Projection / Holdings / Channeling cannot eliminate the practical possibility of meaningful review, February 29, 2000; Stone-Zsela Part II with O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer (five).
- Particular-determination baseline and separate claim limits: same Record, Particular Medicare determinations ordinarily use the prescribed review route; Jurisdictional affirmance preserves the separate limits on claims and relief; Part I, all nine.

**Present operation effective:** Illinois Council, February 29, 2000.

**Exceptions and limits:** The four-Justice regulatory-category alternative is not a controlling exemption and is not aggregated with the Court's rationale. No Mine Act relief mechanism, general immediate-review right, new mandamus duty or guaranteed merits remedy follows.

**Related current rules:** Review of Medicare reimbursement reopening refusals retains its treatment of a particular reopening request after an available original review opportunity; that setting does not establish practical foreclosure.

### Continuing state-judgment injury after the prevailing business closes

**Governing question:** Whether a municipality may obtain federal review of an adverse state judgment after the regulated business has ceased operating.

**Current rule:** A state judgment’s continuing withdrawal of municipal enforcement authority, together with the respondent’s continued adverse defense of that judgment, maintains a live federal controversy despite the respondent’s cessation of the regulated business. The actual legal disability and continuing adversity are necessary; abstract governmental interest, corporate existence, fees or a speculative return to business do not suffice.

**Authority by component:**

- Concrete state-review injury and continued adversity: City of Erie v. Pap’s A. M. — 1. The existing state judgment presents a live federal controversy, March 29, 2000; Stevens’s Part I joined by O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer.

**Present operation effective:** City of Erie, March 29, 2000.

**Exceptions and limits:** This is not a public-law or fee-dispute exception to Article III. The defendant-cessation burden is not transferred to a plaintiff who leaves its business.

### Defaulted ineffective assistance offered as cause for another default

**Governing question:** Whether a constitutional assistance claim may excuse another default when the assistance claim has its own state procedural bar.

**Current rule:** Offering an ineffective-assistance claim as cause does not exempt it from an independent, adequate and properly applied state procedural bar. If that claim is defaulted, the prisoner must excuse its default through cause and actual prejudice or an applicable recognized miscarriage-of-justice gateway before using it as cause for another claim. Exhaustion alone is insufficient because it can reflect expiration of state remedies. The State must establish the asserted independent, adequate and properly applied ground; a successful adequacy challenge removes that bar without a cause showing for it.

**Authority by component:**

- Independent procedural requirements for the assistance claim and distinct excuse routes: Edwards v. Carpenter — A constitutional assistance claim retains its own procedural requirements when offered as cause, April 25, 2000; Souter joined by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Ginsburg.

**Present operation effective:** Edwards, April 25, 2000.

**Burdens and proof:** Cause requires an objective defense-external impediment or qualifying unconstitutional assistance, not ordinary attorney negligence or an assumed collateral-counsel right. Actual prejudice requires actual and substantial disadvantage from constitutional error, not a possibility of harm. The offense-innocence gateway requires reliable new evidence which, with the probative record as a whole, makes it more likely than not that no reasonable properly instructed juror would find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

**Exceptions and limits:** The state rule’s own good-cause exception is distinct from federal cause excusing a valid default. Default remains nonjurisdictional, no universal sequence of habeas defenses is imposed, and a gateway does not establish the constitutional merits or erase independent statutory restrictions.

### Meaningful defense before judgment against a newly added party

**Governing question:** Process required when an amended pleading adds a person against whom an existing judgment is sought.

**Current rule:** Before imposing personal liability on a newly added defendant, the court must give notice of the personal claim and a meaningful opportunity to answer and defend it. Leave to amend and adjudication of that liability are separate acts. Corporate control, testimony for the corporation, resistance to joinder or an appeal after judgment does not alone replace the missing personal defense opportunity. Supported preclusion can limit relitigation but does not eliminate the opportunity to contest its basis and scope.

**Authority by component:**

- Separate amendment and personal adjudication, with the defense opportunity: Nelson v. Adams USA, Inc. — Permission to add a defendant does not adjudicate the personal claim, April 25, 2000; Scalia’s unanimous opinion.

**Present operation effective:** Nelson, April 25, 2000.

**Sequence or decisionmaker:** Then-effective Rule 15(a) allowed the remaining original response period or ten days after service of the amended pleading, whichever was longer, unless the court otherwise ordered. Timing discretion does not permit elimination of meaningful response; no constitutional ten-day minimum follows. Rule 15(b) requires actual express or implied consent to trial of the issue, and corporate participation does not automatically establish consent to personal liability.

**Exceptions and limits:** The decision requires neither a second trial of every corporate issue nor immunity from a properly proved personal obligation. Rule 15(c) relation back does not decide the claim.

### Exhaustion-return applications under former habeas law

**Governing question:** Whether an application renewed after a without-prejudice state-exhaustion dismissal is second or successive under the former habeas rules.

**Current rule:** When an initial federal application was dismissed without prejudice solely to complete state exhaustion before any federal merits adjudication, its renewal remains a first application even if additional grounds are included. Former Rule 9(b)’s new-ground abuse branch does not eliminate the rule’s second-or-successive predicate in that setting. Independent exhaustion, adequate state default, timing and lawful case-management requirements remain applicable; the classification creates neither an unlimited amendment right nor immunity from a genuinely applicable abuse rule.

**Authority by component:**

- Exhaustion-return classification, additional claims and retained independent requirements: Slack v. McDaniel — IV. This exhaustion return remains a first application, including its additional grounds, April 26, 2000; Ginsburg joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Breyer.

**Present operation effective:** Slack, April 26, 2000.

**Exceptions and limits:** Former Rule 9(a) separately permits dismissal when delay prejudices the State’s ability to respond unless reasonable diligence could not have revealed the grounds before prejudice arose. Rule 9(b) permits rather than commands dismissal on its predicates. Former §2244(b)’s prior-merits permission and its conjunctive exception for an unadjudicated ground without deliberate withholding or other abuse are not invoked by an exhaustion dismissal without a merits adjudication.

**Open question:** Slack decides no universal rule for every nonmerits dismissal or later claim, and no amended §2244 authorization determination or exception. The amended statute retains its own applicability and classification predicates.

### Omitted available claims and the section 2255 savings clause

**Governing question:** Whether omission from an earlier merits proceeding makes section 2255 inadequate or ineffective.

**Current rule:** An available claim omitted from an earlier collateral proceeding decided on its merits does not make the section 2255 remedy inadequate or ineffective merely because the prisoner now cannot satisfy the successive-motion conditions. Section 2241 cannot circumvent those conditions on that basis. The All Writs Act likewise supplies no substitute route for the same regulated conviction challenge; an independently authorized remedy must establish its own authority, forum and procedural predicates.

**Authority by component:**

- United States v. Barrett; First Circuit No. 96-2355, 178 F.3d 34; no Supreme Court docket supplied. — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, I. An omitted available claim does not establish an inadequate section 2255 remedy; II. The All Writs Act supplies no substitute for the failed statutory route, 2000-05-22; Ginsburg Part I with all eight other Justices; Part II with all seven other Associates, Stone-Zsela concurring only in that disposition.

**Present operation effective:** 2000-05-22; the component authority identified above.

**Exceptions and limits:** An intervening substantive rule showing noncriminal conduct without an earlier reasonable opportunity remains unresolved. A procedural evidentiary violation is not itself substantive innocence. Authorization-review bars, evidentiary innocence gateways and claims never receiving first merits consideration retain their distinct rules.

**Related current rules:** Federal-prisoner limitation and successive-motion certification supplies the independent authorization conditions and ordinary-review bar.

### Assigned federal financial claims and False Claims Act relator standing

**Governing question:** The injury supporting Article III standing of an FCA relator.

**Current rule:** The FCA partially assigns the United States’ concrete financial claim to the relator, permitting the relator to enforce that assigned interest subject to ordinary injury, causation and redressability requirements and stage-appropriate support. An anticipated reward without an underlying injury would not suffice. The assignment does not make every relator action the United States’ own suit for other legal purposes.

**Authority by component:**

- Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens; No. 98-1828. — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, I. Transfer of the government's financial claim supplies standing, 2000-05-22; Scalia with all eight other Justices.

**Present operation effective:** 2000-05-22; the component authority identified above.

**Exceptions and limits:** Defendant coverage, immunity and Article II control are separate. The holding supplies no general answer for every assignment, penalty-only action or private public-interest claim.

### Private False Claims Act actions against sovereign States

**Governing question:** Whether the FCA authorizes an independently maintained relator action against a sovereign State.

**Current rule:** The generic person language in section 3729, read with the private-relator scheme and section 3733’s investigation-specific definition, does not affirmatively authorize the relator’s private action against a sovereign State. Investigation authority, the State’s potential claimant capacity and partial assignment do not supply that separate defendant coverage. Statutory dismissal on this ground requires no ruling on constitutional immunity.

**Authority by component:**

- Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens; No. 98-1828. — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, II. This private-relator action is not authorized against a sovereign State, 2000-05-22; Scalia with Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer (seven).

**Present operation effective:** 2000-05-22; the component authority identified above.

**Exceptions and limits:** Direct suits by the United States, municipalities, retaliation, differently drafted legislation and Article II remain open. No grant-acceptance consent is inferred, and the existing rule permitting properly authorized Article I enforcement remains effective.

### Whole-record review of a jury verdict under Rule 50

**Governing question:** How a court assesses whether the record can support a jury verdict.

**Current rule:** The court considers the entire record, draws reasonable inferences for the verdict winner and makes no credibility choices or weighing of evidence. It disregards evidence favoring the movant that the jury was free to disbelieve, while considering uncontradicted and unimpeached evidence the jury was required to credit. Disinterested testimony is a relevant circumstance rather than an inflexible witness-label rule. The source of an item alone neither compels belief nor permits its exclusion.

**Authority by component:**

- Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Products, Inc.; No. 99-536. — Canonical Decision Record, Holdings, II. Rule 50 preserves reasonable jury inferences while considering the whole record, 2000-06-12; Scalia with all eight other Justices.

**Present operation effective:** 2000-06-12; the component authority identified above.

**Exceptions and limits:** In discrimination cases, Hicks’s prima-facie-plus-falsity inference remains permissible rather than compulsory. Material falsity need not be supplemented by a special evidence category, but genuinely conclusive contrary evidence can defeat sufficiency; merely imagining another motive cannot. Ultimate persuasion remains with the plaintiff.

**Related current rules:** Claim-specific grounds in renewed Rule 50 motions supplies preservation; Appellate judgment after exclusion of trial evidence supplies the separate appellate authority and new-trial boundaries; Rejected employment explanations and circumstantial discrimination proof supplies the existing Hicks inference.

### Independent departmental authority for a Government criminal appeal

**Governing question:** Whether an asserted United States Attorney appointment defect defeats an appeal independently supported by a lawfully appointed assistant and the Department of Justice.

**Current rule:** An independently appointed assistant's section 542 authority, the Department's section 516 litigation authority, the Solicitor General's criminal-appeal authority under 28 C.F.R. section 0.20(b), and a notice satisfying Rule 3(c) can support the Government's appeal independently of the challenged United States Attorney's appointment. Rule 3(c) does not require that officer's personal signature.

**Authority by component:**

- Independent notice and appellate authority: Canonical Decision Record `United_States_v_Hilario_merits_2001-03-19.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / Independent departmental authority supports the appeal, 2001-03-19; Breyer with all seven other Associates; Stone-Zsela agrees with the result but not this ground.

**Present operation effective:** March 19, 2001.

**Exceptions and limits:** The independent appointments and statutory authority must actually exist. This rule concerns the appeal alone and does not establish independent authorization of an indictment, ratification of a defective act or validity of the challenged appointment.

**Holdings navigation:** [United States v. Hilario — Departmental authority for federal criminal appeals](HOLDINGS.md#united-states-v-hilario-1).


### Later review after an affirmance for want of a quorum

**Governing question:** Review of an antecedent constitutional liability question through a later judgment in the same continuing litigation after a section 2109 no-quorum affirmance.

**Current rule:** An earlier affirmance for want of a quorum does not foreclose consideration of the antecedent constitutional liability questions properly presented on review of the later judgment. The prior statutory affirmance retains its lawful case-specific force and mandate below. The distinction rests on the Court's prior inability to consider either merits or whether to undertake merits review, together with the difficulty of an equivalent substitute for that review.

**Authority by component:**

- Confined section 2109 distinction and retained mandate: Canonical Decision Record `United_States_v_Hatter_merits_2001-05-21.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / I. The earlier statutory affirmance does not bar this later review, 2001-05-21; Souter with Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Kennedy, Ginsburg and Breyer.

**Present operation effective:** May 21, 2001.

**Exceptions and limits:** This does not erase interparty effect of equally divided affirmances after consideration, reopen every unreasoned final judgment, or adopt a general extraordinary-circumstances exception. Ordinary review of a necessary antecedent ruling through a later judgment supplies the lawful channel; it does not alone answer the additional no-quorum issue.

**Holdings navigation:** [United States v. Hatter, 532 U.S. 557 — Later review following a no-quorum statutory affirmance](HOLDINGS.md#united-states-v-hatter-532-us-557-1).


### Final appealability after arbitration and complete dismissal

**Governing question:** Whether an order compelling arbitration and dismissing every claim is appealable under FAA §16(a)(3).

**Current rule:** An order compelling arbitration and dismissing all claims ends the action and is a final decision under §16(a)(3). A possible later award-confirmation or related proceeding does not keep the dismissed action pending. A stay retaining claims is a different interlocutory disposition; final appealability does not establish that dismissal rather than a stay was proper.

**Authority by component:**

- Complete-dismissal finality and stay distinction: Canonical Decision Record `Green_Tree_Financial_v_Randolph_merits_2000-12-11.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / A complete dismissal is a final appealable decision, 2000-12-11; Stevens’s Part I, all nine direct joins.

**Present operation effective:** Green Tree Financial, December 11, 2000.

**Holdings navigation:** [Green Tree Financial Corp.-Alabama v. Randolph, 531 U.S. 79 — Appellate finality of arbitration dispositions](HOLDINGS.md#green-tree-financial-corp-alabama-v-randolph-531-us-79).


### Claim preclusion after federal diversity judgments

**Governing question:** The source and content of a federal diversity judgment’s claim-preclusive effect in another forum.

**Current rule:** Federal common law governs the external claim-preclusive effect of a federal diversity judgment on state-law claims. It ordinarily adopts the preclusion law used by the courts of the State where the rendering federal court sits, unless that law conflicts with a specifically demonstrated federal interest. General uniformity or finality alone does not establish the exception. Rule 41(b)’s merits designation governs rendering-court effect and does not independently extinguish the claim in every other forum. Its default yields to a contrary dismissal order and excludes lack of jurisdiction, improper venue and failure to join a Rule 19 party.

**Authority by component:**

- Federal source, ordinary incorporation and concrete-conflict exception: Canonical Decision Record `Semtek_International_v_Lockheed_Martin_merits_2001-02-27.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / I. Federal law ordinarily adopts rendering-state preclusion for diversity judgments, 2001-02-27; Scalia’s unanimous opinion.
- Rule 41(b) scope, exceptions and separate external effect: the same Record, Holdings / II. Rule 41(b)'s merits designation does not supply universal claim preclusion, 2001-02-27; the same unanimous opinion.

**Present operation effective:** Semtek, February 27, 2001.

**Exceptions and limits:** Section 1738 and the Full Faith and Credit Clause do not directly govern a federal judgment. The rule does not authorize refiling in the rendering federal court or promise an opportunity to relitigate elsewhere. Federal-question judgments and materially different process-sanction dismissals are outside the decision. Whether a rendering federal court may bar refiling when state procedure would dismiss without prejudice is a separate unresolved Rules Enabling Act question.

**Holdings navigation:** [Semtek International Inc. v. Lockheed Martin Corp., 531 U.S. 497 — Claim preclusion of federal diversity judgments](HOLDINGS.md#semtek-international-inc-v-lockheed-martin-corp-531-us-497).


### Judicial estoppel after acceptance of an inconsistent position

**Governing question:** When a litigant’s repudiation of a position judicially accepted in earlier proceedings may be barred.

**Current rule:** A court may prevent a clearly inconsistent position following judicial acceptance of the earlier position when repudiation would produce unfair advantage or impair the earlier adjudication’s integrity. Clear inconsistency, actual judicial acceptance and resulting advantage or detriment guide an equitable inquiry, not an exhaustive formula or inflexible prerequisites. A supported genuine mistake or material change in law, policy or essential fact can affect application. A State invoking judicial relief is subject to this protection of adjudicative integrity.

**Authority by component:**

- Contextual inquiry, genuine explanations and application to a State’s accepted interpretive premise: Canonical Decision Record `new_hampshire_v_maine_merits_2001-05-29.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / Judicial estoppel protects an accepted adjudicative position, 2001-05-29; Kennedy’s opinion joined by all eight participating Justices.

**Present operation effective:** New Hampshire v. Maine, May 29, 2001.

**Exceptions and limits:** Negotiation alone is not judicial acceptance, and every compromise statement is not a binding admission. Different legal labels alone do not establish an actual contradiction. The rule is distinct from claim and issue preclusion; the ordinary effect of changes in government policy remains outside this decision. Estoppel does not enlarge the geographic or substantive scope of an earlier decree.

**Holdings navigation:** [New Hampshire v. Maine, 532 U.S. 742 — Judicial estoppel and accepted interstate positions](HOLDINGS.md#new-hampshire-v-maine-532-us-742).


### Judicial correction of unlawful mushroom assessment rulings

**Governing question:** Review and enforcement after an administrative assessment ruling under the Mushroom Promotion, Research, and Consumer Information Act.

**Current rule:** If an administrative ruling under the Mushroom Promotion, Research, and Consumer Information Act is contrary to law, section 6106(b)(3) requires return to the Secretary for the lawful ruling directed by the court or the further action law requires. Consolidated enforcement must conform to the governing judicial determination.

Section 6106(b)(4)'s rule that mere pendency of an administrative petition does not impede section 6107 enforcement is distinct. It neither permits collection of an obligation adjudged unconstitutional nor decides separately sought interim relief.

**Authority by component:**

- Mandatory lawful administrative return and distinct pending-petition rule: Canonical Decision Record `United_States_v_United_Foods_Inc_merits_2001-06-25.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / III. Affirmance bars the challenged advertising enforcement and requires lawful implementation, 2001-06-25; six direct joins.

**Present operation effective:** 2001-06-25.

**Exceptions and limits:** Accounting, actual severability and monetary recovery require their own legal and factual predicates. No universal refund, fixed collection amount or invalidation of independently lawful Council activity follows from an advertising violation.

**Holdings navigation:** [United States v. United Foods, Inc. — Compelled advertising in an independent market](HOLDINGS.md#united-states-v-united-foods-inc-1).


### Express discovery extensions under an accrual-based filing period

**Governing question:** When discovery extends 15 U.S.C. §1681p’s two-year period measured from liability arising.

**Current rule:** Under §1681p's two-year liability-arising formulation, the period runs from liability arising and carries no general extension until discovery. Its express extension permits filing within two years after discovery only if the defendant materially and willfully misrepresented information the Act required it to disclose to the individual, and that information was material to establishing that defendant's liability to that person. Ignorance of the violation alone meets neither the exception nor an additional discovery rule.

**Authority by component:**

- Canonical Decision Record `trw-inc-v-andrews_merits_2001-11-13.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / No general discovery extension under the governing FCRA; Question left undecided, 2001-11-13; Ginsburg with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Breyer, seven.

**Present operation effective:** TRW Inc. v. Andrews, 2001-11-13.

**Open question:** Whether a particular claim's liability arises only on actual loss remains undecided. This construction establishes no universal accrual or discovery rule for federal statutes; traditional fraud/concealment and distinct statutory regimes retain their own scope.

### Independent and adequate state procedural grounds

**Governing question:** Whether the state procedural ground invoked against a federal claim actually bars federal review.

**Current rule:** A state requirement must be both independent and adequate before its procedural default bars federal consideration. Ordinary validity and regular application do not conclusively establish adequacy when the actual application is exorbitant. Courts must examine the combined circumstances and the work compliance would perform, while respecting the State's construction of its own rules. An inadequate ground requires no additional cause-and-prejudice excuse; removal of that barrier establishes neither the underlying federal violation nor entitlement to habeas relief. A decision on state procedure is not a merits adjudication under §2254(d) simply because it disposed of the appeal.

A state waiver rule does not become dependent on federal merits merely because the required form of waiver turns on the kind of right implicated. Under Arizona Rule 32.2(a)(3)'s authoritative construction for the 1995 petition, rights requiring personal, knowing, voluntary and intelligent waiver are not forfeited by omission alone; identifying that category does not decide the alleged violation. Courts must inspect the actual state order: a procedural ground that actually rests on a federal constitutional ruling is not independent, while a reference to the right or to colorability is not conclusive by itself. This distinction resolves the presented habeas independence inquiry without adopting universal equivalence between direct-review jurisdiction and habeas default.

**Authority by component:**

- Canonical Decision Record `lee-v-kemna_merits_2002-01-22.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / I. This exceptional application of the continuance rules is inadequate to bar federal review; II. Removal of the default barrier returns the distinct constitutional claim, 2002-01-22; Souter with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Ginsburg and Breyer, six.

- Waiver-category identification, the actual-order inquiry and independent remaining default requirements: Canonical Decision Record `stewart-v-smith_merits_2002-06-28.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / I. The clarified waiver rule classifies rights without deciding their violation; II. The actual state order rests on omission and consideration of an excuse; III. Independence is settled, while genuinely remaining requirements retain their own force, 2002-06-28; the unanimous per curiam opinion.

**Present operation effective:** Stewart v. Smith, June 28, 2002, for the waiver-category independence component; Lee v. Kemna, January 22, 2002, for application-specific adequacy and the consequence of an inadequate ground.

**Exceptions and limits:** Lee establishes no general oral-motion, emergency or substantial-compliance exemption. The unexpected absence of subpoenaed trial witnesses, earlier substantive presentation, short requested delay and stated scheduling impediments operated together; no one fact supplies an automatic exception. Independent exhaustion and habeas restrictions remain applicable. Resolving independence does not reopen an otherwise settled adequacy determination or establish cause; properly preserved cause-and-prejudice or miscarriage-of-justice issues retain their own requirements. A valid, applicable, preserved and unexcused default must be enforced.

**Related current rules:** Sequencing nonretroactivity and procedural default on habeas review governs order and judicial initiative, not the adequacy of a particular state ground.

### Supplemental-claim tolling and sovereign immunity

**Governing question:** Whether §1367(d) tolls limitations for an immune state-law claim against a nonconsenting State.

**Current rule:** The tolling provision does not cover a state-law claim excluded from §1367(a)'s supplemental adjudicative grant by the State's sovereign immunity. Original jurisdiction over a valid federal claim does not itself bring the separate immune state claim within that grant or its linked tolling protection. Immunity is assessed claim by claim.

**Authority by component:**

- Canonical Decision Record `raygor-v-regents-of-university-of-minnesota_merits_2002-02-27.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / Supplemental tolling does not cover this nonconsenting State’s immune state-law claims, 2002-02-27; Thomas with O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Ginsburg, five.

**Present operation effective:** Raygor v. Regents of University of Minnesota, 2002-02-27.

**Open question:** The constitutional power to enact a differently specified tolling rule is undecided. The valid federal ADEA remedial channel is not withdrawn.

### Complaint-based patent appellate jurisdiction and transfer

**Governing question:** Whether a patent counterclaim supplies specialized arising-under jurisdiction and how an appeal filed in the wrong circuit is preserved.

**Current rule:** Under then-operative sections 1295(a)(1) and 1338(a), a patent counterclaim alone, even compulsory, does not make an action arise under patent law when the plaintiff's well-pleaded complaint contains no patent-law basis. A counterclaim remains an independent controversy but cannot supply that specialized appellate allocation; the district court's independently established jurisdiction over the action is unaffected. When an appellate court lacks jurisdiction, section 1631 requires transfer if the receiving court could have heard the appeal when noticed and transfer serves justice. The appeal then proceeds using the original notice date.

**Authority by component:**

- Complaint-based allocation: Canonical Decision Record `holmes-group-inc-v-vornado-air-circulation-systems-inc_merits_2002-06-03.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / I. A patent counterclaim does not supply the incorporated arising-under basis, 2002-06-03; Stone-Zsela with Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Breyer.
- Transfer conditions and original-date preservation: Canonical Decision Record `holmes-group-inc-v-vornado-air-circulation-systems-inc_merits_2002-06-03.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / II. The appeal must be transferred to the Tenth Circuit, 2002-06-03; all nine.

**Present operation effective:** Holmes Group, Inc. v. Vornado Air Circulation Systems, Inc., 2002-06-03.

**Open question:** Materially amended plaintiff pleadings require their own jurisdictional record; the rule resolves no general category beyond counterclaim-only jurisdiction.

### Appeal by an objecting member of a mandatory class

**Governing question:** Whether a timely objector bound by a mandatory class settlement must intervene before appealing its approval.

**Current rule:** An unnamed mandatory Rule 23 class member who timely objects to settlement approval binding that member's own rights is a party for the limited purpose of appealing the approval without separately intervening. Ordinary appellate requirements and preservation remain. This appellate status does not grant general control of the class action, reopen a concluded intervention denial or decide the objections' merits.

**Authority by component:**

- Binding mandatory adjudication and limited appellate party status: Canonical Decision Record `devlin-v-scardelletti_merits_2002-06-10.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / Limited appellate party status follows this mandatory adjudication of the objector's own rights, 2002-06-10; Ginsburg with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter and Breyer.

**Present operation effective:** Devlin v. Scardelletti, 2002-06-10.

**Related current rules:** Intervention before a shareholder's derivative-settlement appeal retains Felzen's distinct derivative-shareholder rule. Devlin establishes no general opt-out-class rule.

## Civil rights and constitutional remedies

### Individual-capacity liability for official conduct under §1983

**Governing question:** Whether use of official authority prevents a state officer from being a §1983 person when sued individually.

**Current rule:** A state officer sued in an individual capacity is a person under §1983 even when the challenged act was undertaken through official authority; sovereign immunity does not independently bar a judgment payable by the officer personally. The plaintiff must prove the officer's own federal violation under color of law, and applicable personal immunities remain available. The capacity in which the officer is sued, rather than whether the conduct was official, distinguishes this action from a claim against the State or an official-capacity damages claim.

**Authority by component:**

- Personhood, capacity distinction, personal-payment immunity limit, and retained defenses: Hafer v. Melo — Individual-capacity §1983 coverage of official conduct, November 5, 1991; O'Connor's unanimous participating opinion.

**Present operation effective:** *Hafer*, November 5, 1991.

**Holdings navigation:** Hafer v. Melo, 502 U.S. 21 (1991) — Individual-capacity liability.

### Municipal responsibility and the underlying federal deprivation

**Governing question:** The distinction between an underlying federal deprivation and municipal responsibility, including final policymaking for the challenged function.

**Current rule:** A municipal employee who proves deprivation of a federal right under color of state law and the required municipal responsibility need not prove an additional, independent abuse-of-governmental-power element. The federal deprivation and its attribution to municipal policy or custom remain separate required inquiries. Employment alone establishes neither municipal liability nor a substantive right; *Canton*'s training analysis supplies attribution and causation, not the underlying constitutional guarantee. For a final-policymaker theory, the court identifies through state and local law, including custom or usage with legal force, who speaks finally for the particular entity on the challenged subject. Final operational discretion does not alone answer that question; labels, election, territory, financing or lack of commission control is individually insufficient. An Alabama sheriff's independent local office supplies County final law-enforcement authority in the criminal-investigation function addressed in McMillian, even without commission delegation or review. An attributable policy or final decision must still cause the proved federal injury. For a training or supervision omission, the plaintiff must establish a deliberate or conscious municipal choice amounting to deliberate indifference, an identified deficiency closely related to the federal injury, and actual causation. Notice can come from an established pattern or an obvious need to address a clear constitutional duty in known recurring circumstances; prior identical incidents are not invariably necessary. Negligence, a single employee’s error, general supervisory responsibility and hindsight that additional training might have helped are insufficient. Responsibility for police conduct requires actual supported authority over that conduct rather than cooperation alone.

Consequential examination injuries caused by a proved municipal removal-policy violation do not invariably require proof of a second examination policy. The underlying wrong, municipal causal connection, injury and recoverable measure must nevertheless be established separately for each consequence. That route does not authorize adjudication of an unpresented independent examination-policy claim or adopt a constitutional rule for such examinations.

**Authority by component:**

- Rejection of the additional element and separation of deprivation from attribution: Collins v. City of Harker Heights — No extra governmental-abuse element under §1983, February 26, 1992; Part A of Stevens's opinion, joined by all nine Justices.

- McMillian v. Monroe County — I. Final authority and the government represented are distinct inquiries, 1997-06-02; Ginsburg, all nine
- McMillian v. Monroe County — II. The sheriff's independent local office supplies County law-enforcement authority, 1997-06-02; Ginsburg with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter and Breyer; five
- McMillian v. Monroe County — III. The County claim returns for the remaining liability elements, 1997-06-02; the same five

- Deliberate omission, notice, identified deficiency and causation: Carter v. City of Philadelphia — A deliberate municipal omission must actually cause the constitutional injury, March 13, 2000; Ginsburg’s opinion joined by all seven other Associate Justices.

- Consequential injury from an established municipal wrong without an invariably required second policy: Canonical Decision Record `Wallis_v_Spencer_merits_2001-04-02.md`, Public Projection / Holdings / III. The independent examination theory requires a threshold determination, while consequential injury remains possible, 2001-04-02; all nine.

**Present operation effective:** Wallis, April 2, 2001, for the consequential-injury qualification; the existing Collins, McMillian and Carter attribution and fault components retain their stated authority.

**Current wording authority:** Carter, March 13, 2000, states the surviving Canton training-and-supervision requirements and applies them without adopting a separate Walker test.





**Exceptions and limits:** Other sheriff functions, other States' arrangements, individual liability and State liability or immunity require separate analysis. Institutional identity does not prove the truth of misconduct or make every official act municipal policy. Bryan County's pending reargument supplies no hiring, fault or causation change.

**Holdings navigation:** [Wallis v. Spencer — Emergency child removal and municipal responsibility](HOLDINGS.md#wallis-v-spencer).


### Voluntary public employment and substantive workplace safety duties

**Governing question:** Whether a voluntary public-employment relationship creates a general substantive-due-process duty to provide workplace safety.

**Current rule:** Voluntary municipal employment does not itself create the custody or deprivation of liberty that supports affirmative constitutional duties of care, and substantive due process imposes no independent general obligation to provide such employees a workplace free from unreasonable risks. A state-law safety duty, even assuming it creates a protected liberty interest, does not convert its breach alone into a substantive constitutional wrong. The underlying federal right and constitutional arbitrariness remain distinct from state-law entitlement and municipal attribution.

**Authority by component:**

- No employment-based general safety duty or custody: Collins v. City of Harker Heights — Voluntary public employment creates no general constitutional safety duty, February 26, 1992; Part B of Stevens's unanimous opinion.
- State entitlement does not alone establish arbitrary deprivation: Collins — These pleaded omissions do not establish constitutional arbitrariness, February 26, 1992; Part C joined by White, Blackmun, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, and Thomas with Stevens. Stone's distinct concurrence is not part of this component's authority.

**Present operation effective:** *Collins*, February 26, 1992.

**Open question:** Actual compulsion, deliberately inflicted bodily injury, procedural due process, and a properly alleged affirmative-danger claim are not resolved. *Collins* creates neither a general affirmative-danger test nor a categorical rejection of one.

**Holdings navigation:** Collins v. City of Harker Heights, 503 U.S. 115 (1992) — Municipal liability and public employment.

### Compensatory remedies for intentional Title IX discrimination

**Governing question:** Whether remedial silence or Spending Clause notice bars compensatory damages in the established Title IX private action.

**Current rule:** When a cognizable federal statutory cause of action exists, courts may award appropriate relief absent clear congressional direction limiting it; recognizing relief does not itself create a new cause of action. Title IX's established private action permits compensatory damages for proved intentional discrimination, subject to proof of recipient responsibility, causation, and compensable loss. The Spending Clause notice principle does not categorically bar that compensation for intentional breach of Title IX's express nondiscrimination condition.

**Authority by component:**

- Appropriate relief in an existing action and availability of Title IX compensation: Franklin v. Gwinnett County Public Schools — Compensatory relief in the established Title IX action, February 26, 1992.
- Rejection of the categorical funding-notice bar: Franklin — Notice does not bar damages for the pleaded intentional violation, February 26, 1992. Both holdings rest on White's opinion joined by Stone, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, and Souter; Scalia and Thomas supply judgment votes only on a narrower statutory ground.

- Kinman v. Omaha Public School District — III. Recipient compensation requires its own culpable response, 1997-05-27; five direct joins supply the teacher-harassment recipient rule
- Sufficient actual-notice recipient-own-wrong route for controlled peer harassment: Canonical Decision Record `davis_v_monroe_county_board_of_education_merits_1999-05-24.md`, Holdings / A school's own culpable response can support damages for controlled peer harassment, 1999-05-24; Ginsburg Part I with Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter and Breyer, six direct joins. The distinct educational-harm component is stated in the related peer-harassment rule.

**Present operation effective:** Franklin, 1992-02-26, for the remedy-availability rule; Kinman, 1997-05-27, resolves the separate teacher-harassment recipient standard; Davis, 1999-05-24, supplies the separately stated sufficient controlled-peer route.

**Open question:** Recipient attribution in settings not resolved by the teacher-harassment rules or Davis's sufficient actual-notice route for controlled peer harassment, punitive relief, unintended discriminatory effects and genuinely ambiguous funding conditions remain unresolved.

**Related current rules:** Teacher harassment and recipient responsibility under Title IX supplies Kinman's controlling recipient standard. [Recipient responsibility for peer harassment under Title IX](#recipient-responsibility-for-peer-harassment-under-title-ix) separately states Davis's sufficient route and its limits.

**Holdings navigation:** Franklin v. Gwinnett County Public Schools, 503 U.S. 60 (1992) — Statutory discrimination remedies. Kinman v. Omaha Public School District (1997-05-27) — Civil Rights / Teacher harassment and institutional responsibility. [Davis v. Monroe County Board of Education — A school's own culpable response can support damages for controlled peer harassment](HOLDINGS.md#a-schools-own-culpable-response-can-support-damages-for-controlled-peer-harassment-1).

### Private enforcement of Adoption Assistance Act reasonable-efforts and reporting clauses

**Governing question:** Private enforcement of 42 U.S.C. §671(a)(15)'s reasonable-efforts clause and §671(a)(9)'s reporting clause through §1983 or an action implied directly under the Act.

**Current rule:** Read within the Act's plan and administrative-enforcement structure, §671(a)(15) creates no individual right enforceable under §1983 to compel the asserted reasonable efforts to prevent removal or reunify families. An approved plan's commitment, §671(a)(3)'s statewide-operation requirement and caseworker deficiencies do not supply that missing right. Nor does §671(a)(15) imply a separate private action: beneficial purpose does not establish congressional intent to create the requested remedy. Section 671(a)(9) requires a plan to provide reporting to the appropriate court or law-enforcement agency when a state agency has reason to believe a child's home or institution is unsuitable because of neglect, abuse or exploitation and the child's care is paid for in whole or in part under Title IV-E or IV-B. That administrative direction does not create the asserted private §1983 right or an implied action to obtain caseworker relief. The §1983-right and implied-action inquiries remain distinct; failure to imply an action does not bar an otherwise available enacted §1983 remedy.

**Authority by component:**
- No individual §671(a)(15) right: Suter v. Artist M., March 25, 1992, “Section 671(a)(15) supplies no individual reasonable-efforts right enforceable under §1983,” Part II.
- No separate implied (15) action: the same record, “Section 671(a)(15) supplies no separate implied action,” Part III.
- Reporting trigger and absence of asserted §1983 right: the same record, “The asserted §671(a)(9) reporting claim is not enforceable through §1983,” Part IV-A.
- No implied reporting action: the same record, “The asserted §671(a)(9) claim supplies no separate implied action,” Part IV-B. White for O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas supplies six controlling joins for each component.

**Present operation effective:** Suter, March 25, 1992.

**Exceptions and limits:** No general rule makes state-plan provisions unenforceable. Administrative funding review does not necessarily foreclose an otherwise existing §1983 right, and the State's administrative obligations remain. Appropriate relief presupposes a cognizable action and cannot create the missing right or action.

**Open question:** Private enforceability of §671(a)(16), read with §675(1) and §675(5)(B), remains undecided, as do the preserved claim's merits and proper relief.

**Holdings navigation:** Suter v. Artist M., 503 U.S. 347 (1992) — Child-welfare statutory enforcement.

### Private use of state seizure procedures and qualified immunity

**Governing question:** Whether private litigants using state replevin, garnishment or attachment procedures receive public-official immunity under Harlow.

**Current rule:** Private litigants invoking those procedures do not receive Harlow's objective immunity from suit merely because qualifying joint action is attributable to the State under §1983. State attribution and immunity eligibility remain separate; reasonable reliance on legislation does not itself establish this immunity. Each defendant's attribution and other liability predicates still require independent determination.

**Authority by component:**
- Private-immunity exclusion and separate attribution: Wyatt v. Cole, “Private litigants and immunity from suit”, May 18, 1992; O'Connor, joined in full by White, Blackmun, Stevens, Scalia and Kennedy (six); Stone adds a join only for replevin and the reservations (seven at that scope).

**Present operation effective:** Wyatt v. Cole, May 18, 1992.

**Open question:** The existence and scope of a distinct good-faith or probable-cause defense, any additional plaintiff's elements and allocation of any such burden remain undecided. Eligible public officials' immunity is unchanged.

**Holdings navigation:** Wyatt v. Cole, 504 U.S. 158 (1992) — Section 1983 immunity.

### Ordinary pleading and substantive proof requirements

**Governing question:** Whether substantive liability or evidentiary frameworks justify heightened pleading beyond the Federal Rules in municipal civil-rights and employment-discrimination actions.

**Current rule:** Courts may not impose a judge-created heightened factual-particularity requirement on municipal §1983 complaints beyond the then-operative Federal Rules. Rule 8 governs; Rule 9(b)'s fraud-or-mistake categories do not add municipal liability. Monell and Canton retain their substantive attribution and causation requirements. Rule 11, discovery control and Rule 56 remain distinct. No individual-officer pleading standard is decided.

A Title VII or ADEA plaintiff need not plead each element of the McDonnell Douglas prima facie evidentiary framework. Rule 8 requires a short, plain statement giving fair notice of the challenged employment decision, alleged prohibited basis and grounds of the claim. The proof framework belongs to evidence, not a mandatory complaint checklist. This does not remove substantive elements or the distinct operation of Rule 11, discovery management and summary judgment.

**Authority by component:**
